sections.b: Twelve psalms carry Asaph's name: Psalm 50 and Psalms 73 to 83, which open Book III of the Psalter. They have a character of their own. They speak often of God as judge, use the image of Israel as God's flock (Psalm 74:1; 77:20; 78:52; 79:13; 80:1), retell the exodus and wilderness (Psalms 77, 78, 80, 81), and name Joseph and the northern tribes (Psalm 77:15; 78:67; 80:1–2). Several mourn the temple's destruction (Psalms 74, 79), so many scholars read "of Asaph" as the name of the singers' guild, which still existed after the exile (Ezra 2:41), rather than of David's singer himself. Harry Nasuti and Michael Goulder argue that the Asaph tradition began among northern Levites. Chronicles' picture of Asaph as one who "prophesied" (1 Chronicles 25:2) fits psalms in which God speaks directly (Psalm 50; 75:2–5; 81:6–16; 82).

common: Asaph was one of David's three chief singers, and his family led temple music for centuries.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Asaph psalms first took shape among Levites of the northern kingdom and came to Jerusalem after 722 BC.

sections.b: Psalm 73 tests the belief that God rewards the good. The singer kept his heart clean, yet he was struck every morning, while the arrogant stayed healthy and rich (Psalm 73:3–14). His answer does not deny what he saw. In God's holy places he saw the end of the wicked, "turned to waste in an instant" (Psalm 73:19), and found that God himself was his share forever (Psalm 73:26). The reward is redefined: "Drawing near to God is my good" (Psalm 73:28).

Praying over the burned temple, the singer of Psalm 74 recalls God's oldest victory: "You split the Sea by your strength. You shattered the heads of the dragons on the waters. You crushed the heads of Leviathan" (Psalm 74:13–14). Leviathan has several heads, like Lotan, the seven-headed serpent of the Ugaritic poems, and like the dragon of Revelation 12:3. The victory is followed by the ordering of creation (Psalm 74:15–17). The psalm uses the old picture to argue that the God who defeated chaos once can do it again.

sections.h: Psalms 74 and 79 and the Maccabean crisis
sections.b: 1 Maccabees quotes Psalm 79:2–3 when Alcimus has sixty Hasideans killed (1 Maccabees 7:16–17), and Psalm 74's burned gates, profaned sanctuary and absence of prophets resemble 1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:38, 46. Theodore of Mopsuestia and some modern scholars therefore dated both psalms to the 160s BC. Most scholars think they were written after 587 BC and reapplied by the Maccabean generation, which shows how the psalms were prayed again in new disasters.

sections.b: Psalm 78 calls manna "heaven's grain" and "the bread of the mighty ones" (Psalm 78:24–25), which the Greek rendered "bread of angels". The crowd in John 6:31 quotes "He gave them bread from heaven to eat", a form of Psalm 78:24, and Jesus answers that he is the true bread from heaven. In the Talmud (Yoma 75b) Rabbi Akiva took the "mighty ones" to be angels, and Rabbi Ishmael read it as bread wholly absorbed by the body.
sections.refs: Psalm 78:23–25; Exodus 16:4; John 6:31–35; Wisdom of Solomon 16:20

sections.b: Psalm 78:43–51 lists seven blows: blood, the swarm, frogs, locusts, hail on vines and trees, hail (or, with a one-letter change, plague) on the livestock, and the death of the firstborn. Gnats, boils and darkness are missing, and the order differs from Exodus 7–12. Psalm 105:28–36 gives another selection, beginning with darkness. The psalms retell the plagues as poetry, choosing and arranging them; some scholars think they also reflect forms of the tradition older than the final book of Exodus.

Psalm 78 explains the end of Shiloh as God's judgment: "He left the tabernacle of Shiloh behind, the tent where he had made his home among humankind. He let his strength be taken captive" (Psalm 78:60–61). The verses follow 1 Samuel 4: the ark captured, the priests killed by the sword, Phinehas's widow dying (Psalm 78:62–64). The psalm then sets Shiloh against Zion: God rejected Joseph's tent and chose Judah and Mount Zion (Psalm 78:67–68). Jeremiah later used Shiloh as a warning to Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:12–14).

Psalm 78:61 calls the captured ark God's "strength" and "beauty": God let his own glory go into captivity. Psalm 80:1 calls God the one who sits on the cherubim as his throne, the ark's title in 1 Samuel 4:4.

Psalm 78 ends its long history with God's choice of David: "he took him from the pens where the sheep were kept ... to be shepherd over Jacob, his people" (Psalm 78:70–71), following the promise of 2 Samuel 7:8. Placed at the start of Book III, the hope prepares for Psalm 89, where the same promise seems broken.

"He turned down Joseph's tent; Ephraim's tribe was not his choice. He chose Judah's tribe instead, Mount Zion, the one he loved" (Psalm 78:67–68). Psalm 78 tells election as history: God's choice of Zion and David answers Israel's repeated failure. Genesis already sets Ephraim's blessing (Genesis 48:20) beside Judah's scepter (Genesis 49:10).

In the middle of Psalm 78's story of rebellion stands a verse of mercy: "Yet he is compassionate; he makes atonement for guilt and does not destroy. Many times he turned his anger back and did not rouse all his fury" (Psalm 78:38). It opens the Jewish weekday evening prayer and was recited during judicial flogging (Mishnah Makkot 3:14). It answers Psalm 77:9's fear that anger had locked up God's compassion.

Psalm 80 tells Israel's history as the life of a vine: dug up from Egypt, planted after the nations were cleared, rooted, filling the land from the Sea to the River (Psalm 80:8–11). Now its walls are down and a wild hog from the woods chews it (Psalm 80:12–13). The people ask God to "tend this vine" and to strengthen "the son", a word that can mean a branch (Psalm 80:14–17).

sections.h: "The son of man you made strong" (Psalm 80:17)
sections.b: Psalm 80:17 prays for "the man of your right hand ... the son of man you made strong for yourself". In the psalm the phrase means a human being, most likely the king or Israel itself. The Targum reads the parallel line of Psalm 80:15 as "the King Messiah", and Christians have heard Jesus, the Son of Man at God's right hand (Mark 14:62).

Psalm 79 asks God to "pour out your fury on the nations that have not known you" (Psalm 79:6) and to repay the neighbors sevenfold (Psalm 79:12). The prayer comes from a people whose dead lie unburied in Jerusalem (Psalm 79:2–3), and it asks God to act, not Israel. 79:6–7 is read at the Passover Seder when the door is opened for Elijah.

Book III (Psalms 73–89) begins with eight psalms of Asaph. Psalm 73 tests the faith of Psalm 1. Psalms 74 and 79 mourn the burned temple; 75 and 76 answer with God's judgment and his defense of Zion; 77 turns a night of doubt into a hymn of the exodus; 78 retells Israel's history from Egypt to David; and 80 prays for the northern tribes. The book will close with Psalm 89's lament over the fallen house of David.

sections.h: "Is his loyal love gone for good?" (Psalm 77:8)
sections.b: In a sleepless night the singer of Psalm 77 questions God's creed of Exodus 34:6, word by word: loyal love, graciousness, compassion (Psalm 77:7–9). The answer comes not as an argument but by remembering the exodus (Psalm 77:11–20). Psalm 79:2 calls the dead of Jerusalem God's "loyal ones" (chasidim), people of hesed.

Psalm 78 tells the wilderness years as the story of a people who could not trust: water from the rock (Psalm 78:15–16), the demand for meat (Psalm 78:18–20), manna and quail (Psalm 78:23–29), the plague at Kibroth Hattaavah (Psalm 78:30–31), and forty years spent "in emptiness" (Psalm 78:33). It draws on Exodus 16–17 and Numbers 11, 14 and 20, in its own order.

sections.h: Laments of the community in Book III
sections.b: Psalms 74, 79 and 80 are laments of the whole community: the temple burned (Psalm 74), Jerusalem's dead unburied (Psalm 79), the northern tribes ravaged (Psalm 80). They ask "Why?" and "How long?" (Psalm 74:1, 10; 79:5; 80:4), remind God of his past acts and his name, and end in a promise of praise. Psalm 77 shows the same movement in one person's night.

sections.h: The cup in the LORD's hand (Psalm 75:8)
sections.b: "For the LORD holds a cup in his hand, its wine foaming, full of spiced mix ... its dregs they will drain and drink, all the wicked of the earth" (Psalm 75:8). The cup of wrath reappears in Jeremiah 25:15, Isaiah 51:17 and Revelation 14:10.

Psalm 76 pictures God as a lion with his lair in Salem and his den in Zion, from which he breaks the weapons of war (Psalm 76:2–3). With Psalms 46, 48 and 87 it is one of the Songs of Zion. Psalm 78:68 calls Zion the mountain God loved.

sections.h: Psalm 80: a prayer for Joseph's tribes
sections.b: Psalm 80 calls on the Shepherd of Israel before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh (Psalm 80:1–2), probably during the Assyrian attacks that ended the northern kingdom in 722 BC. The Greek title adds "about the Assyrian".
